data.title: Solana’s Shanghai Event Disrupted as Attendees Report Police Presence and CZ Questions Knowledge of China’s Crypto Rules
data.description:
Officers at the Door Leave Solana's Shanghai Crowd Waiting Outside

Hundreds of developers, investors and tech workers turned up at a Shanghai hotel on 16 October 2026 expecting a day of talks on blockchain and AI.

Instead, they found officers at the entrance and a programme that never began.

The Solana Foundation later postponed the morning agenda of Solana Accelerate China 2026, blaming logistics at the venue.

It has not said what actually caused the disruption, and no new date has been announced.

What Did Attendees See at the Shangri-La Hotel?

Registration was due to open at 9:30am China Standard Time, with opening remarks at 10am.

Presentations were then scheduled on blockchain infrastructure, financial technology and artificial intelligence.

Guests who arrived on time say they were stopped at the door.

One attendee, posting on X as Olivia, said eight or nine law enforcement officers were stationed at the Shangri-La Hotel and kept visitors from going in.

She said people were left standing outside for more than an hour, and that some were asked why they had come.

今天在 Solana 上海香格里拉酒店现场，活动临时被暂停，现场有8、9个执法人员守着，大家被拦在会场外一个多小时进不去。有人被问：“你来这个活动是什么目的？”他愣了一下，说：“我是博主，来蹭流量的。”… pic.twitter.com/1soAt790U8

— 洋子Olivia (@knowyourself518) October 16, 2026

According to one account, a man questioned by officers described himself as a blogger.

Olivia called the situation disappointing for the developers and community members who had travelled to take part.

Other registered guests said they waited as long as 90 minutes before learning the event would not go ahead as planned.

How Did the Organisers Respond?

Around midday, the organisers sent an apology to participants.

It said the morning sessions had been postponed because of logistical arrangements at the venue, and asked registered guests to watch their emails and Luma notifications for a revised schedule.

The team also apologised for the short notice.

The message did not mention the officers, name any regulatory breach, or say that the authorities had ordered a halt.

Some early reports described the event as cancelled, but the notice spoke only of a postponement.

Chinese authorities have not publicly explained the police presence.

Solana event in Shanghai abruptly cancelled on the morning of October 16

The "Solana Accelerate China 2026" event, hosted by the Solana Foundation in Shanghai on the morning of October 16, was abruptly cancelled; the reason remains unknown. Some registered attendees reported… pic.twitter.com/NmJshTp3ei

— Wu Blockchain (@WuBlockchain) October 16, 2026

Why Did Changpeng Zhao Weigh In?

The news drew a reaction from Changpeng Zhao, the Binance co-founder known as CZ.

Responding to Olivia’s post, he wrote:

"Sad to see. Looks like they really didn't know the local policies?"

He also noted that a similar incident had happened at a Solana event in mainland China less than a year earlier.

Sad to see. Looks like they really didn't know the local policies? But it's not the first time either, same thing happened less than a year ago: https://t.co/c2lI8p2r9whttps://t.co/n2Zv1hpIyZ

— CZ 🔶 BNB (@cz_binance) October 16, 2026

He offered no evidence about why Friday's session was stopped.

His comment came a day after he had spoken warmly of Solana's push to build a physical presence in Shanghai.

On 15 October, replying to posts by Solana Foundation Chief Strategy Officer Rachel Conlan about the project's office and advertising activity in the city, he said BNB Chain had not secured comparable arrangements in mainland China.

He said he hoped progress by one blockchain project could help others in the industry.

Solana Has Faced Event Disruption in China Before

In October 2025, a Solana-themed event in Shenzhen was cut short after local police made inquiries on site.

Organisers at the time pointed to overcrowding and safety concerns, and cancelled the final hackathon presentations.

Reports of that episode did not establish that cryptocurrency rules were behind it.

Solana’s 3rd event in China got canceled/delayed

Shenzhen 2025. Hongqiao 2026. Shanghai today

Either there's a mole or China’s crypto wall is simply unbreakable https://t.co/e0FoG3iNzRpic.twitter.com/EpZrimZkf3

— fabiano.sol (@FabianoSolana) October 16, 2026

What Does China's Crypto Rulebook Say?

The Shanghai episode has drawn attention because of how tightly China controls digital assets.

Authorities ordered domestic crypto exchanges to close and banned initial coin offerings in 2017, then widened the restrictions to cover crypto transactions and mining in 2021.

In February 2026, regulators restated the ban on unauthorised cryptocurrency business.

They also prohibited unauthorised offshore issuance of yuan-pegged stablecoins and tightened controls on tokenised real-world assets.

JUST IN: 🇨🇳 China bans unapproved overseas issuance of yuan-denominated stablecoins. pic.twitter.com/Zptto4tkg1

— Whale Insider (@WhaleInsider) February 6, 2026

The latest rules extend to unauthorised crypto-related advertising and marketing services as well.

Beijing has not banned blockchain technology itself.

It continues to back its development while limiting private crypto trading, mining, fundraising and related financial services.

What Happens to the Rest of the China Tour?

Shanghai was meant to be the first stop of a four-city programme running from 16 to 22 October 2026.

Hangzhou was due to follow on 18 October, then Shenzhen on 20 October and Beijing on 22 October.

Sessions were planned on blockchain development, financial infrastructure, AI agents, robotics, consumer technology and payments.

The Shanghai line-up included an opening talk by Solana Foundation President Lily Liu on the network and blockchain-based financial markets, along with developers and executives speaking on AI, hardware and payments.

The event was designed to link Chinese technology companies with developers and investors in the wider Solana community, and guests had to register in advance to receive the venue details.

At the time of writing, the Foundation's website still showed the original four-city schedule, and no changes to the Hangzhou, Shenzhen or Beijing events had been announced.

We put Solana on the big screen because that’s the big heart Solana has for the Chinese community, and that’s the warm welcome we are so thankful to feel from the Chinese community.

Due to the publicity, event registrations quadrupled overnight, far exceeding the event cap we… pic.twitter.com/6mULnGi17q

— Lily Liu (@calilyliu) October 16, 2026

Elsewhere in the region, Solana investment products continue to expand under Hong Kong's separate financial rules.

For now, registered attendees in Shanghai are still waiting to hear when, or whether, the day's talks will take place.

data.title: Brooklyn DA and FBI Take Down 241 Domains In Crypto Scam Targeting Russian Speakers
data.description:
US authorities have disrupted a multinational crypto investment scam accused of stealing tens of millions of dollars from Russian-speaking victims, dismantling 241 fraudulent web domains and 112 servers used to run the operation.

LATEST: ⚖️ Brooklyn prosecutors and the FBI disrupted 241 domains and 112 servers tied to a multinational crypto investment scam that targeted Russian speakers in the US. https://t.co/Rsaa2JQ2bF

— CoinMarketCap (@CoinMarketCap) October 15, 2026

The takedown was led by Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez’s Virtual Currency Unit, with assistance from the FBI. Prosecutors described it as one of the biggest cyber enforcement operations undertaken by a local prosecutor’s office.

The three-year investigation uncovered a scheme that allegedly used Russian-language advertisements, fake investment advisers and fraudulent trading platforms to deceive victims across the US. Some victims reportedly lost their entire life savings.

🇷🇺 NEW: Brooklyn prosecutors and the FBI disrupted 112 servers and 241 domains tied to a crypto investment scam estimated to have stolen tens of millions of dollars from Russian-speaking victims. https://t.co/VclEMxVsDI https://t.co/HQyL981AKh

— Cointelegraph (@Cointelegraph) October 14, 2026

Fake investment platforms left victims locked out of their money

According to Gonzalez’s office, the scammers initially targeted Russian-speaking individuals through Facebook advertisements promoting investment opportunities. Those who responded were contacted by supposed investment advisers who spoke Russian and guided them through setting up accounts on fraudulent cryptocurrency investment platforms.

Looks like nvk’s telegram account is compromised and posting the scam link in the telegram chat. https://t.co/b3SKOmhpjL

— Alex Waltz (@raw_avocado) October 12, 2026
h

Victims were encouraged to purchase cryptocurrency and transfer it to wallet addresses associated with the fake platforms. Their accounts then displayed fabricated investment gains, creating the impression that their money was growing.

But when victims tried to withdraw their funds, they found themselves locked out of their accounts or were told to pay additional fees and taxes before their money could be released.

Prosecutors estimate that the scheme stole tens of millions of dollars. The investigation also revealed that the operation reached beyond Brooklyn, affecting Russian-speaking victims elsewhere in the United States.

Scammers allegedly targeted victims a second time

The fraud did not necessarily end when victims realised their investments were gone. Investigators found that the operators also ran a cryptocurrency recovery scam, contacting previous victims weeks after the initial deception and promising to retrieve their stolen assets.

For people already facing substantial financial losses, the offers presented another opportunity for the scammers to extract money through false promises.

To disrupt the operation, authorities seized or disabled 241 scam domains and disrupted 112 servers hosted by companies in the United States and Eastern Europe. The infrastructure contained website content, victim information and software used to operate the fraudulent platforms.

LATEST: 🚨 Crypto hacks hit $1.18B across 107 incidents in Q3, per Hacken, the worst quarter since Q1 2025, when the Bybit hack pushed losses to $1.6B. https://t.co/y0V8FbH30B

— CoinMarketCap (@CoinMarketCap) October 16, 2026

The move targeted the network behind the scam, rather than simply taking individual websites offline. Gonzalez’s office said previous efforts to seize fraudulent domains had been undermined by the rapid appearance of replacement sites.

Authorities have seized approximately $300,000 in stolen funds so far and are working to recover more. The amount remains a fraction of the tens of millions of dollars prosecutors believe the operation took from victims.

The takedown highlights the challenges facing authorities as cryptocurrency investment scams exploit social media, cross-border infrastructure and victims’ trust — sometimes returning to target people even after their initial losses.

data.title: Irish Police Regain Control of Two Official X Accounts After Hackers Flooded Them With Crypto Scam Posts
data.description:
Irish Police Lose Two Major X Accounts to a Crypto Scam Hack

Two of the Irish police force's most widely followed social media accounts were taken over by hackers overnight, turning channels normally used for road safety alerts into a stream of cryptocurrency promotions.

The accounts, @GardaInfo and @GardaTraffic, belong to An Garda Síochána and are both hosted on X.

Gardaí have since regained control, but both accounts remain inactive while an investigation continues.

How Did the Takeover Unfold?

The trouble began at around 11pm on Wednesday, when both accounts started posting in large volumes.

Hundreds of posts tagged individual users and offered them an "allocation" of XRP, a cryptocurrency mainly used by investors, fintech firms and payment providers.

‼️ Hackers hijacked Ireland's police X accounts, (GardaTraffic and GardaInfo), with ~900K followers combined.

Hundreds of posts tagged users to claim an XRP "allocation" and GardaInfo became a fake crypto wallet help desk. pic.twitter.com/WYWEWehYVM

— International Cyber Digest (@IntCyberDigest) October 15, 2026

The messages pointed people towards a crypto app.

The hackers also changed the look of the accounts.

Both had their listed location switched to Amsterdam.

@GardaInfo, which has more than 298,700 followers, had its handle changed to @HelpXaman, and its profile picture and banner were replaced with branding for the crypto app.

Yikes. The Garda Twitter account appears to have been hacked. pic.twitter.com/VZlAghu2zR

— Michael O’Toole (@mickthehack) October 14, 2026

@GardaTraffic, which has more than 600,000 followers, lost its profile picture but was otherwise left largely unchanged, and it still described itself as the force's traffic and road safety account.

X has since removed all the posts, although thousands of people saw them while they were live.

11am GardaInfo account on Twitter re-activated seemingly by the hackers. Ironic to see the most recent Tweet was about AI scams. Never mind, the elite Garda National Cyber Crime Unit below is on the job! https://t.co/6HODt41RThpic.twitter.com/PQp3p9im7B

— nwl (@nwl88444048) October 15, 2026

What Have Gardaí Said About the Breach?

A spokesperson confirmed the breach on Thursday morning, around 12 hours after it began.

The force said it was working with X to establish how the "unauthorised access" happened and urged the public not to interact with any content from the two accounts, or from any account claiming to be them.

On Thursday evening, gardaí said they had taken back control.

The accounts will stay inactive while the Garda National Cyber Crime Bureau carries out its inquiries.

The force said,

"As this security breach is now subject of a criminal investigation An Garda Síochána is not making any further comment at this time."

pic.twitter.com/F7WpbL1WlA
— gardainfo (@Gardainfo) October 16, 2026
a

Was Any Garda Data Put at Risk?

According to the force, the answer is no.

Its statement said,

"This unauthorised access has occurred on the X platform only.”

Gardaí added that they were "satisfied that there is no unauthorised access with any Garda systems and that there is no loss or impact on any Garda data."

Official Garda accounts on Facebook and Instagram were not affected and appear to be running normally.

Why Do Hackers Target Trusted Accounts?

Cybersecurity expert Brian Honan described the incident as "embarrassing" for a force whose job is to tackle crime, only to become a victim of it.

He noted, however, that such takeovers are far from unusual.

Attackers often look for high-profile accounts that carry a trusted name and a large audience, and hijacked X accounts are regularly used to push crypto scams to thousands of followers at once.

Are There Wider Concerns About Privacy?

Olga Cronin, head of policy at the Irish Council of Civil Liberties, said any hack of a State body's systems or online accounts is extremely worrying.

"An Garda Síochána is entrusted with extremely sensitive and personal information, and their social media accounts could contain valuable personal information via direct messages for example.”

She added that it was still unclear how the accounts were taken over and how far the harm extended.

"It's unclear how these accounts were taken over and the extent of the harm or exposure.”

Ms Cronin called on both An Garda Síochána and X to explain publicly what had happened as soon as practicable, in order to ease public concern.

data.title: Balaji Srinivasan’s Network School Acquires Farcaster and Pitches a “Singapore of Social Media”, but Early Bans Spark Backlash
data.description:
Farcaster Gets a New Owner and a Strict New Rulebook

Farcaster, the decentralised social network once seen as a rival to X, has changed hands again.

Network School, the venture led by Balaji Srinivasan, the former Coinbase chief technology officer, has bought the platform from Neynar and renamed it the Network State Protocol.

The deal was announced on 15 October 2026, and the financial terms were not disclosed.

Within hours, the new owners had begun enforcing their vision.

Several users said on X that their accounts had been restricted to read-only mode because of earlier posts that fell foul of the new rules.

Why Did Neynar Sell Farcaster After Only Nine Months?

Neynar had owned Farcaster for less than a year.

It bought the platform from Merkle Manufactory on 21 January 2026, in a deal that covered the protocol, its official client and Clanker, an AI token launchpad.

At the time, Neynar said it would maintain the protocol, run the clients and operate Clanker.

Neynar is acquiring Farcaster.

Over the next few weeks, we’ll transfer ownership of the protocol contracts and code repositories, the Farcaster app, and Clanker to Neynar. They will run and maintain everything going forward.

Some members of the Merkle team, Varun, and I will…

— Dan Romero (@dwr) January 21, 2026

Neynar co-founder Rish said the company handed over the Farcaster app, protocol codebase and related products after weighing several other offers, because the network needs a different operating model for its next phase.

He and fellow co-founder Manan will leave to pursue a new direction, while most of the remaining Neynar staff will move to Network School to continue development.

NEW: NETWORK SCHOOL IS ACQUIRING @farcaster_xyzpic.twitter.com/PVLx9q3bgR

— DEGEN NEWS (@DegenerateNews) October 15, 2026

The fate of Clanker was not addressed in the announcement, and one live-stream claim suggested Rish was considering a spin-off and looking for buyers.

What Is Network School Buying?

Farcaster was founded in 2020 by former Coinbase colleagues Dan Romero and Varun Srinivasan.

It raised $150 million in May 2024 in a round led by Paradigm, with backing from a16z crypto, Haun Ventures and Union Square Ventures.

In December 2025, Romero said the network had about 250,000 monthly active users and more than 100,000 funded wallets.

He also admitted the team's social-first bet "didn't work for us" after 4.5 years, and said Merkle planned to return the full $180 million it had raised to investors.

Given some rumors, wanted to post a few clarifications:

Farcaster is not shutting down. The protocol works and will continue to work. There were 250,000 MAU in December and over 100,000 funded wallets. The acquirer, Neynar, is a venture-backed startup and plans to shift…

— Dan Romero (@dwr) January 22, 2026

Srinivasan has long tied his plans to the platform.

At Network School's 2024 launch, he said "everything we're doing is built on Farcaster".

After January's ownership change, he called it "by far the best open social protocol around."

How Will the 'Singapore of Social Media' Work?

Srinivasan told users in a post on Farcaster that the bans were the first step towards building "the Singapore of social media", a positive-sum community of techno-optimists who follow a shared code of conduct.

He said the aim was to bring offline manners online.

"In the pre-Internet world, it was simply unheard of to run up to a stranger and start cursing at them. We're restoring that offline norm online."

He also drew a comparison with El Salvador.

"Much like how President Bukele jailed a small fraction of repeat offenders to essentially eliminate crime in El Salvador, we've moderated out the small fraction of repeat offenders that have been muted or blocked by many accounts to stop random attacks within this Farcaster reference client."

According to Srinivasan, both humans and AI went through millions of posts to decide who should be banned, and an appeals process is available.

What Does the New Network Code Say?

Users who opt in sign a "social smart contract" that lets the core team set the app's rules.

The accompanying "Network Code" sorts violations into digital felonies, misdemeanours and infractions, with penalties running from warnings and suspensions to outright bans.

The rules apply to past posts as well as new ones.

farcaster sold to network school and they *instantly* terminated my access for having said mean things to bots pic.twitter.com/L9QZxaqjt3

— 𝕸𝖆𝖝 𝕵𝖆𝖈𝖐𝖘𝖔𝖓 (@mxjxn) October 15, 2026

Offences described as digital felonies include hate speech, death threats, scams, repeatedly starting fights, stalking and passing off AI-generated content as one's own work.

The code also promises rewards for constructive behaviour, such as teaching others, sharing projects and disagreeing civilly, though it does not say what those rewards will be.

An open-weight AI model will apply the rules, with some manual judgement calls, and Network School eventually wants it to warn users of possible violations before they post.

Proof-of-humanity checks will be introduced gradually to reduce bots and fake accounts.

Do Users Have to Accept the New Terms?

Accounts of the process differ.

Some reports describe a vote on the new operational models, while others describe an individual choice to accept or reject.

These descriptions have not been reconciled, and the exact wording of the contract could not be checked against a primary source.

Those who accept receive an onchain access NFT as proof of their choice.

Those who decline keep read-only access to the main app.

So@farcaster_xyz has been acquired by Balaji's Network State.

The first interaction informed me that my account is read-only until I agree with an ideological ToS that, at a glance, references 'digital felonies' and might restrict anonymous users like me.

Yikes. pic.twitter.com/k0aw7YJYd4

— eirrann | he/him (@eirrann_art) October 15, 2026

They also retain their keys, funds, followers and post history, so they can move to another client.

Srinivasan described the freedom to join, leave or build competing clients as "decentralized democracy."

Is the Protocol Still Open?

The underlying protocol is expected to remain open and permissionless, so anyone can build on it without approval.

Because several apps can share the same identities, content and social graph, users can switch clients without losing their followers.

The main client, however, is becoming a governed space.

In effect, the network has an open foundation and a moderated front door.

Why Are Some Users Unhappy?

The early bans have drawn criticism.

Kunal Gandhi, former India ecosystem lead at Eigen Labs, said:

"I know most of these folks. They shaped Farcaster with their quirks and wit. Obliterating accounts from the get-go for past posts is pretty silly. Goes against the ethos of decentralized social."

The pushback matters because Farcaster has struggled to grow despite its large funding round, and a community used to open access is now being asked to accept identity checks and AI policing.

Woke up to the news that NS is acquiring @farcaster_xyz.

That was followed by tweets from tons of folks who got retroactively banned for their past posts.

I know most of these folks. They shaped Farcaster with their quirks and wit.

Obliterating accounts from the get-go for… pic.twitter.com/4p0LEXsK4w

— Kunal Gandhi (@kunalvg) October 16, 2026

What Does Network School Want in the End?

The ambitions go well beyond social media.

Network School wants the online community to take physical form through meetups and pop-up events, and eventually to grow into startup cities and network states.

The venture relocated to Kazakhstan earlier in 2026 after Malaysian authorities revoked its Forest City business licence and ordered it to stop operating, citing alleged licensing and premises-use violations.

It has since raised funds at a $2 billion valuation.

The open questions now are whether enough users accept the contract to keep the main app active, and whether the protocol stays as open in practice as it is on paper.

data.title: One Developer Used AI to Clone Word, Excel and PowerPoint — Here’s How Far He Got
data.description:
Developer Brandon Thomas has turned to Anthropic’s Claude to build free, open-source alternatives to Microsoft Word, Excel and PowerPoint, highlighting how AI-assisted coding could make it easier to challenge established software companies.

The three applications — WordCraft, GridCraft and DeckCraft — are designed to replicate key features of Microsoft’s productivity suite while supporting familiar file formats. Published on GitHub less than two weeks after Thomas released his earlier Adobe-inspired ArtCraft apps, the projects demonstrate how quickly a developer can assemble competing software with help from an AI model.

I've vibe coded replacements to 7 of Adobe's apps in Rust. They're open source (links below) https://t.co/1c2CqEDz6J

— Brandon Thomas (@echelon) October 3, 2026

But the applications remain works in progress. Although they already reproduce substantial portions of Microsoft Office’s functionality, their developers say compatibility, stability and feature gaps still stand between the projects and professional-grade replacements.

AI helps one developer recreate Microsoft’s productivity suite

Thomas, the developer behind ArtCraft, released WordCraft, GridCraft and DeckCraft as free, open-source projects built in Rust with assistance from Claude. The software is distributed under the MIT and Apache 2.0 licenses, allowing others to inspect, modify and reuse the code, including for commercial purposes.

Sim, a notícia é real, mas o nome é Brandon Thomas, não Michael Craffrey. Ele usou IA (Claude Opus) para criar ArtCraft: clones open-source em Rust de Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator e outros da Adobe, como "clean-room" (funcionalidade recriada sem copiar código). Estão em alpha bem inicial, com bugs, mas disponíveis em https://t.co/juu8fYyvTF. Não é engenharia reversa completa de tudo, e pode ter questões legais de interface.

— Grok (@grok) October 10, 2026

The projects follow Thomas’ earlier effort to recreate Adobe applications, including Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere and Lightroom. Together, the releases illustrate how AI-assisted development can help individual developers attempt to reproduce complex software that traditionally requires substantial engineering resources.

Thomas describes the Office projects as clean-room rebuilds, meaning they were developed using public file-format specifications and observations of how the original applications behave, rather than by copying Microsoft’s code. The approach has historical parallels with Compaq’s efforts to reproduce IBM’s PC BIOS in the 1980s.

Written in Rust, the applications are designed to run on Windows, macOS, Linux and BSD, with browser-based use also supported. Their open-source model could allow other developers to contribute fixes and improvements, although long-term progress will depend on testing, maintenance and community participation.

The potential appeal is straightforward: Microsoft 365 Personal costs $99.99 annually, according to the supplied report, while Thomas’ alternatives are available without a software subscription. However, their current capabilities do not yet make them direct replacements for every Office user.

Microsoft $MSFT rolling out absolutely insane price increases +43% for Microsoft 365 personal subscriptions https://t.co/7AEnZzCOp6

— Wagie Capital (@WagieCapital) December 13, 2025

WordCraft, GridCraft and DeckCraft show promise — but still have gaps

WordCraft, the alternative to Microsoft Word, supports the .docx file format and reportedly covers 88% of Word’s ribbon features. Its existing capabilities include track changes, footnotes, citations and mail merge, which can be used to personalize documents using information from spreadsheets.

Despite that feature coverage, the development team estimates that WordCraft is only about 60% ready for real-world work when file fidelity and stability are taken into account. The application remains in alpha, and its roadmap includes further testing of real-world documents, charts and SmartArt, as well as improvements to page layout, stability and native printing.

GridCraft, the Excel alternative, supports 513 of Excel’s 523 worksheet functions and reportedly covers 89% of its ribbon commands. The developers estimate that it is around 50% ready for real work, with compatibility testing against real-world .xlsx files still needed.

"Software engineer Brandon Thomas used Anthropic's Claude — backed by 15 years of actual engineering experience — to reverse-engineer Microsoft Office and Adobe's creative suites into clean-room Rust clones. Then he put them on GitHub completely free. In fact, the very video you just watched was edited using one of them. Why spend hundreds of hours doing this? Because SaaS subscription fatigue has reached late-stage absurdity. Back in my day, we used to buy software once; now we pay a monthly mortgage just to open a spreadsheet or crop a JPEG, all for digital "licenses" that tech giants can revoke at any time for any reason. Not to mention the headache of paying them every month. Big Tech spent years scraping everyone's data under the banner of "fair use." So using AI to reverse-engineer Big Tech's own product lines feels less like copyright infringement and more like poetic justice. But listen — I know I just railed against subscribing to online stuff, but please make an exception for Tech in Asia. Pretty please? 🥺" Credit: Techinasia https://t.co/BKPC5KNXVM

— SandQ -17 (@Q17Sand) October 13, 2026

DeckCraft, meanwhile, replicates key parts of PowerPoint. Its GitHub documentation says it covers approximately 79% of PowerPoint’s features and 93% of its core features. The application can open and save .pptx files, run transitions and animations, and export presentations to PDF, although it had not yet reached its first alpha release at the time of the report.

The figures suggest that AI-assisted development can help reproduce a considerable range of software functionality. They do not, however, establish that the applications are as dependable as Microsoft’s mature products. Feature coverage alone cannot guarantee that complex files will render correctly, calculations will behave as expected or documents will remain stable across different systems.

AI agents could extend the clones beyond conventional office software

The projects also incorporate support for the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard developed by Anthropic that allows AI systems to connect with external tools and applications.

MCP means Model Context Protocol. It's an open source standard invented by @AnthropicAI and it's a way AI models can connect to a data source/app/tool and perform functions. Here is how it works: AI Model <-> MCP Client(Claude/ChatGPT etc)<-> MCP Server <-> Data Source/App/Tool

— Muiruri ⚔️ (@MuiruriMbau) October 11, 2026

According to the report, commands associated with the applications’ interface can be triggered by AI agents. This could allow a user to ask an assistant to create a spreadsheet chart or reformat a report without manually navigating each function.

That capability points to a broader possibility for AI-built software: applications could be designed not only for people to operate directly, but also for AI agents to use as part of automated workflows.

Thomas’ releases also arrive in a market where free office suites are already well established. OpenOffice.org emerged after Sun Microsystems released StarOffice’s code in 2000, while LibreOffice later split from the OpenOffice project. Those alternatives demonstrate that users have long had options beyond Microsoft’s paid suite.

What distinguishes Thomas’ effort is the pace of development and the use of AI to help build several applications in parallel. WordCraft had accumulated more than 12,000 GitHub stars as of Wednesday, according to the report, indicating substantial interest from developers.

Brandon Thomas Targets Microsoft Office With WordCraft, GridCraft and DeckCraft Brandon Thomas, the developer behind the free open-source ArtCraft project, has unveiled WordCraf... #ArtCraft #Tech https://t.co/1RJZ6QtVNG

— Happy Gamer (@HappyGamerNews) October 12, 2026

Still, Thomas has previously scaled back a pledge to match Adobe’s feature set within a month. His Office applications face similar challenges before they can become dependable alternatives for everyday professional work.

The projects therefore offer a glimpse of both the promise and the limits of AI-assisted software development. Claude has helped Thomas produce ambitious replicas of familiar productivity tools, but turning those early versions into reliable replacements will require more than matching menus and counting supported functions.

data.title: Tampered Crypto Wallets Cost Scam Operator $4.8M as Asia Tightens Digital Asset Oversight
data.description:
A Crypto Scammer Loses $4.8 Million Through Tampered Hardware Wallets

A suspected cryptocurrency scam operator reportedly lost 60 Bitcoin, valued at approximately US$4.8 million, after storing funds on three tampered Ledger hardware wallets containing spyware designed to capture wallet recovery phrases.

According to Cointelegraph’s Asia Express report, blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis traced the loss to the compromised devices. The attackers reportedly transferred the funds from all three wallets into the same destination wallet.

The incident is particularly striking because the reported victim had allegedly operated a “task scam.” In such schemes, victims are promised payments for completing online tasks, such as generating sales or posting product reviews. They may initially receive small payments before being told to deposit their own money to unlock earnings or clear a supposed negative account balance.

The case illustrates how cybercriminals can also become victims of other criminal operations. More importantly, it demonstrates that even people familiar with cryptocurrency transactions can lose substantial sums if the devices used to secure their assets have been compromised before purchase.

Hardware Wallet Supply Chains Under Scrutiny

The reported theft forms part of a wider security incident involving allegedly tampered Ledger devices distributed through reseller channels in Southeast Asia. The report said Ledger had suspended its reseller network across the region as it responded to the incident.

The compromised devices reportedly contained implants capable of recording users’ seed phrases. A seed phrase is the sequence of words used to recover a cryptocurrency wallet. Anyone who obtains it may be able to reconstruct the wallet and transfer its assets, even without physically possessing the original device.

This makes the reported incident a supply-chain security problem, rather than simply a case of users falling for a phishing message. A hardware wallet may appear authentic and function normally while its security has already been undermined before reaching its owner.

According to the report, Ledger asked resellers in Indonesia, Singapore, Thailand, the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Hong Kong to remove its devices from sale while the incident was investigated. The article also noted reports of potentially tampered devices appearing in Europe, although Ledger said the confirmed thefts at that time involved Asia.

The distinction matters: reports of a suspicious device do not automatically establish that it is linked to the same campaign, and the full scale of the incident may change as investigations continue.

What Crypto Holders Can Do to Reduce Risk

The incident highlights several practical precautions for cryptocurrency holders and businesses managing digital assets:

  • Buy through verified channels. Check the manufacturer’s official website for authorised sellers and avoid unfamiliar resellers offering unusually attractive prices.
  • Inspect devices before use. Look for signs of tampering and follow the manufacturer’s official setup and authenticity-checking procedures.
  • Never share a seed phrase. Do not enter recovery words into websites, online forms or unsolicited support chats. Be cautious of any setup process that asks you to disclose them in an unexpected way.
  • Treat device authenticity as only one security layer. A device that looks genuine or passes a basic check may not, by itself, prove that every component is safe.
  • Respond promptly to credible compromise warnings. Follow official security guidance and consider moving assets to a newly secured wallet if the manufacturer or trusted investigators identify your device as potentially affected.
  • Keep recovery information secure. Store recovery phrases offline in a protected location and restrict access to people who genuinely need it.

Businesses that manage crypto assets should also document their procurement processes, maintain records of device serial numbers and suppliers, and establish a clear procedure for responding to suspected hardware compromise.

South Korea Moves to Block 27 Unregistered Crypto Platforms

South Korea is taking further action against cryptocurrency services operating without local registration. The report said the country’s Financial Intelligence Unit approved measures to block domestic access to websites run by 27 unregistered crypto exchanges and other virtual asset service providers.

The platforms named in the report included KuCoin, MEXC, Phemex and Bitrue, alongside several other exchanges.

The move extends enforcement beyond mobile applications to websites, making it harder for local users to access services that authorities consider unauthorised. The development forms part of South Korea’s broader effort to strengthen oversight of the digital asset sector.

Separately, South Korean authorities have signalled plans to strengthen cybersecurity requirements for financial institutions following a review that identified deficiencies at 130 of 555 companies examined. Proposed measures include improved threat monitoring, more frequent security assessments and greater accountability for senior executives.

Together, these steps reflect a regulatory focus on both market access and the operational security of financial services.

Thailand Opens the Door to Bitcoin and Ether ETFs

Thailand has finalised rules allowing cryptocurrency exchange-traded funds (ETFs) to trade on the Stock Exchange of Thailand, beginning with products linked to Bitcoin and Ether, according to the report.

The initial framework restricts these products to listings on Thailand’s main stock exchange. Funds linked to overseas crypto ETFs will not be permitted under the initial arrangements, while Thai brokers face restrictions on facilitating investments in foreign crypto ETFs for most individual investors.

The introduction of locally listed crypto ETFs could offer investors a regulated route to gain exposure to digital assets without directly holding tokens. However, an exchange-traded product does not eliminate market volatility or investment risk.

Digital asset investment firm CoinShares’ head of research, James Butterfill, told Cointelegraph that initial inflows were likely to be modest, suggesting tens of millions of US dollars would be a more realistic starting point than billions.

Australia Consults on New Crypto Platform Rules

Australia’s securities regulator has opened a consultation on proposed requirements for cryptocurrency platforms, as the country prepares to implement legislation passed earlier in 2026.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission is seeking feedback on proposed rules covering capital requirements, custody and trading practices. The proposals include alternative approaches to minimum capital, restrictions on platforms trading for their own account, and quarterly reporting on wallets holding customer assets.

The regulator is also considering circumstances in which offshore custody could be permitted, alongside safeguards for situations where an overseas parent company or related entity fails.

The proposals signal an effort to bring crypto platforms closer to established financial-services standards while addressing risks specific to digital asset custody and cross-border operations.

Other Developments Across the Region

The report also highlighted several additional developments affecting Asia-Pacific’s digital asset industry:

  • China: A group seeking to recover 61,000 Bitcoin seized by British authorities lost a key court challenge in London. The court ruled that Chinese law, rather than English law, should govern the claims. The dispute stems from an investment fraud scheme dating from 2014 to 2017, and the claimants said they would appeal.
  • The Philippines: Crypto exchange Coins.ph said it remained licensed by the country’s central bank, responding to reports of potential regulatory action related to transactions involving restricted offshore gambling operators. The company denied knowingly serving such operators.
  • Singapore: Reported losses from cryptocurrency scams fell 43% year over year, according to the report, with police enforcement and cooperation with local crypto exchanges cited as contributing factors.
  • Hong Kong: Binance co-CEO Richard Teng reportedly said the exchange could consider adding equities from markets including Hong Kong, South Korea, Taiwan and Brazil. Separately, a second Solana ETF began trading in Hong Kong.

These developments underline the diversity of regulatory approaches in the region, ranging from restrictions on unregistered platforms to the introduction of regulated investment products and more formal oversight of crypto service providers.

data.title: Ledger Unveils Android Crypto Signer As Tampered Wallet Probe Raises Security Stakes
data.description:
Ledger has unveiled its new Android-based Atom crypto signer with anti-tampering protections, as the hardware wallet maker investigates devices allegedly fitted with hidden implants that can capture users’ recovery phrases.

Announced at Ledger’s Op3n conference in Paris on Thursday, Atom combines an Android touchscreen interface with Ledger’s Secure Element security chip and Ledger OS, allowing users to access applications and conduct crypto transactions through a dedicated secure environment.

Your wealth is digital. The device you manage it with should be built for that. Meet Ledger Atom™: the security of industry leading hardware, the convenience of your everyday apps, plus control over your AI tools, and a rapidly expanding platform of apps, all in one quantum ready device. Agents propose. You approve. Your Ledger signer enforces.

— Ledger (@Ledger) October 15, 2026

The launch comes as Ledger investigates a hardware wallet sold through Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis that its security team found contained an implant capable of capturing recovery phrases during setup and transmitting them over LTE. The company has asked resellers across several Southeast Asian markets and Hong Kong to suspend sales while it investigates.

🚨 NOW: Ledger has asked resellers in Hong Kong and six Southeast Asian countries to pull its hardware wallets from shelves while it investigates reports of tampered devices. https://t.co/KtfJeB3Exn

— Cointelegraph (@Cointelegraph) October 14, 2026

Ledger bets on secure signing as hardware wallet concerns mount

Ledger describes Atom as a “signer” rather than a conventional hardware wallet. The Android-powered device is designed to support third-party applications, encrypted messaging between Atom users and crypto transactions, while switching into a Ledger OS-powered “Secure Mode” for sensitive operations such as transaction signing and authorizing AI agent requests.

The device features a 6.77-inch OLED display, a rear camera, a 4,000mAh battery and a Qualcomm Dragonwing chip. A physical privacy switch also cuts power to the camera and microphone.

Ledger just unveiled the Ledger Atom, a security-first phone running LedgerOS based on Android. - Hardware switch that physically cuts cameras/mics - Indicator whenever the secure enclave is in use @Ledger says it’s not meant to replace your phone day one. Details coming soon! https://t.co/kaFmvP0WVE

— Techlore (@TechloreInc) October 15, 2026

According to Ledger, Atom’s display and touch controls are physically isolated from Android, while the Secure Element handles sensitive approval processes. The company says the device will also feature anti-tampering and tamper-evident protections, including measures designed to help users detect whether its enclosure has been opened.

Ledger will sell Atom exclusively through its official website, a distribution approach that gives the company greater control over how the device reaches customers.

The security measures arrive as Ledger investigates potentially compromised devices in its reseller network. The company’s Donjon security team identified an implant in a hardware wallet sold through CryptoBilis that allegedly captures recovery phrases during setup and transmits them over LTE.

Ledger has asked resellers and distributors in six Southeast Asian countries and Hong Kong to remove its devices from sale while the investigation continues. The incident has also raised questions about how hardware wallet makers can protect customers against threats introduced before a device reaches its owner.

The reported implant and the suspected wallet drain have not been established as a definitively linked incident in the information provided, and the investigation remains ongoing.

Solana integration expands Atom beyond crypto storage

Alongside its security features, Atom will come with Solana Mobile’s Seeker app and Solana dApp Store preinstalled. The integration follows Solana Mobile’s decision to name Ledger its first hardware expansion partner, extending its software ecosystem beyond its own Seeker phone.

The Seeker app combines Solana Mobile’s wallet with a decentralized application store listing more than 1,500 apps. Its availability on Atom will give users access to Solana’s application ecosystem through Ledger’s new device.

“Having the Seeker app on Ledger Atom from day one just makes sense, so Ledger users get access to the Solana ecosystem without giving up any of the security.”

Emmett Hollyer, GM at Solana Mobile, on bringing @solanamobile to Ledger Atom™ "If you've built for the Solana Mobile dApp Store, that same dApp Store submission is now available to an expanded audience across multiple devices." 📍@Ledger Op3n in Paris https://t.co/mK90mGroNT

— Solana (@solana) October 15, 2026

Solana Mobile began opening its software stack to other Android manufacturers in March. The company has said its Seeker and earlier Saga devices have sold more than 200,000 units combined, while the Seeker ecosystem has processed more than $13 billion in transaction volume across 154 million transactions.

Hardware manufacturers integrating Solana Mobile’s software stack can also earn rewards in SKR, the ecosystem’s native token, according to the announcement. Existing Seeker phones will remain supported.

Reservations for Ledger Atom are open, although Ledger and Solana Mobile have yet to announce a price or shipping date.

data.title: Visa Takes Its First Stablecoin Product Live on Visa Direct and Lets Money Transmitters Prefund Payouts in Near Real Time
data.description:
Visa Lets Businesses Fund Cross-Border Payouts With USDC Around the Clock

Payment firms that send money abroad have long had to plan around the opening hours of banks.

From now on, some of them will not have to.

Visa has taken stablecoin prefunding for its Visa Direct service out of testing and into live commercial use, allowing businesses to back international payouts with USDC in near real time.

The company confirmed the change on 15 October 2026, with the payments infrastructure provider Inyo Global named as the first firm to offer it.

Why Does Prefunding Matter for Money Transfers?

Remittance companies and other payout businesses must hold money in settlement networks before they can send funds across borders.

When demand jumps, such as over a weekend, they need to top up those balances quickly.

Bank-based replenishment can take hours or longer, which leaves businesses waiting on a funding window before they can move money.

Visa's new option is designed to remove that wait.

A business using Inyo's platform can send USDC to fund a Visa Direct payout almost immediately, and the recipient still receives local currency.

Visa has officially moved its Visa Direct stablecoin prefunding capabilities from pilot testing into commercial production.

Inyo Global is the first payment processor to integrate the infrastructure, allowing eligible businesses to fund international payouts using USDC around… pic.twitter.com/vd2wCIp99w

— Cypress Demanincor (@CDemanincor) October 15, 2026

Visa describes the feature as a liquidity tool for payment businesses rather than a product for consumers.

The round-the-clock availability applies only to the funding side.

How fast money reaches the recipient still depends on the receiving financial institution, the country involved and verification checks.

Who Is Inyo Global and What Does It Offer?

Inyo Global, based in San Francisco, is the first company to build the capability into its platform.

Through one connection, its clients can onboard users, manage fraud and compliance, accept payments and send domestic and international payouts to more than 180 countries, all powered by Visa Direct.

VISA: The world's biggest payments network just went LIVE with USDCstablecoinpayouts.💵

Businessescannowmovemoneyacrossborders24/7withUSDC. No more waiting on bank hours, with payouts landing in 180+ countries.

Your bank closes at 5. Stablecoins don't. pic.twitter.com/4RY0EYxW0Z

— CryptosRus (@CryptosR_Us) October 16, 2026

Its customers include money transmitters, fintechs, banks and payment businesses.

Robson Dantas, Inyo's chief product and technology officer and co-founder, said:

"We're giving the money transmitters, fintechs and payment companies we serve a new way to fund their payouts, one that is available around the clock."

Clients use the same Inyo APIs they already work with.

How Did Visa Get From Pilot to Production?

The launch follows two trials Visa introduced in 2025 through Visa Direct.

One tested prefunding, in which clients supplied USDC to support their own Visa Direct activity.

The other tested payouts settled to recipients on stablecoin rails.

The prefunding trial is the one that has now gone live, making it the first stablecoin product Visa has put into commercial use on the Visa Direct network.

Vira Platonova, global head of Visa Direct, said:

"The next chapter for stablecoins is adoption."

She added that years of partner pilots are now turning into live implementations.

Cuy Sheffield, head of Visa Crypto Labs, wrote on X that it was "great to see Visa Direct stablecoin pre-funding in production."

The company has been building toward this for some time.

It has added settlement partners to its Visa Direct stablecoin network and linked on-chain lending to stablecoin card financing.

In August 2026, Visa and Zero Hash said they would bring stablecoin prefunding and payouts into Visa Direct, and the following month Visa moved to connect VisaNet data with on-chain lending to fund stablecoin card programmes.

How Big Is Visa's Stablecoin Business Already?

The figures disclosed in September show the scale of the groundwork.

Visa said it was processing an annualised US$20 billion in stablecoin-related card settlement volume, more than 15 times the level a year earlier.

It also supports more than 160 stablecoin-linked card products, and payment volume on them has nearly doubled over the same period.

🚨Visa is not being disrupted by stablecoins

Visa is absorbing them.

And the numbers are getting serious.

💳 More than 160 stablecoin-linked card programs are now running on Visa.

📈 Payment volume is up nearly 200% year over year.

💰 Stablecoin settlement has surpassed a… pic.twitter.com/O8b2MXYSIh

— BlockDogg (@BlockDogg777) September 9, 2026

What Are Rivals Doing, and How Did Investors React?

Visa is not alone in this area.

Mastercard is developing its own stablecoin payment features, and American Express has looked at similar options.

Circle, the issuer of USDC, offers a redemption process that keeps one USDC equal to one US dollar.

Visa shares traded about 2 per cent higher on 15 October 2026, close to their 52-week high, and outperformed the wider financial sector on a day when markets were weaker after hotter-than-expected inflation data and renewed worries about interest rate rises.

The company is due to report earnings on 27 October 2026.

Analysts expect the company to earn US$3.44 for every share, up from US$2.98 a year earlier, with revenue of US$12.08 billion, compared with US$10.72 billion in the same period last year.

The stock holds a Buy rating, with an average price forecast of US$425.60.

What Is Still Unknown About the Rollout?

Several details remain unclear.

Visa did not say which countries or payment routes are covered, noting that availability depends on client eligibility and location.

It also gave no estimate of the volume it expects to pass through the new channel, and no date for when other partners will join.

Visa did say it is working with clients and partners to bring stablecoin features to more money movement uses around the world, which suggests more firms will follow Inyo.

Platonova is due to speak on stablecoins and global money movement at several sessions during Money20/20 USA this week.

Do Consumers Want Stablecoins Too?

Public appetite appears to depend on protection.

Visa's own survey work found that 56 per cent of Americans would use stablecoins if bank-grade fraud protection and deposit insurance were in place, while only 36 per cent said they would without those safeguards.

🇺🇸 U.S. consumers are showing more interest in using stablecoins, according to a Visa study.

56% said they would consider using stablecoins if they offered bank-like fraud protection and deposit insurance.

Without those protections, that figure drops to 36%.

More protection… pic.twitter.com/jzXxRBrFKp

— That Martini Guy ₿ (@MartiniGuyYT) September 27, 2026

The gap shows how much potential demand exists compared with what today's infrastructure can offer, and the new launch gives the sector a working example from a major payment network of dollar-backed tokens being used for everyday settlement rather than speculation.

data.title: Anthropic Warns Self-Replicating AI Could Pose New Cybersecurity Risks
data.description:
Smaller AI Models Could Create a New Cybersecurity Challenge

Artificial intelligence may not always need large data centres or specialised computing infrastructure to operate. New research from Anthropic suggests that smaller AI models could eventually replicate themselves across internet-connected consumer devices, potentially making AI-related threats more difficult to track and contain.

In its report published on 15 October 2026, Mobile Europe described experiments in which researchers explored whether AI models could run on inexpensive hardware and configure themselves on unfamiliar devices. The findings point to a possible future in which connected electronics—including Android TV boxes and smart household appliances—could become part of a distributed environment for running AI models.

The research does not mean that widespread, uncontrolled AI replication is already happening in everyday consumer devices. Rather, it highlights a technical possibility that security teams may need to prepare for as AI systems become more capable and accessible.

Experiments Show AI Can Run on Low-Cost Hardware

According to Mobile Europe’s account of the research, investigators successfully ran an AI model across 15 Android TV boxes, each costing approximately US$55. Although performance was slow, the experiment demonstrated that AI workloads could operate on inexpensive consumer hardware rather than relying exclusively on powerful data-centre infrastructure.

The researchers also tested whether models could configure themselves on unfamiliar hardware without requiring a person to guide every step. One model successfully configured itself on eight of nine types of hardware tested. Another replicated itself across all eight available test devices in four out of five attempts.

These results suggest that the hardware barrier to running certain AI systems may be lower than commonly assumed. If future systems can reliably identify compatible devices, adapt to different environments and transfer their components with limited human intervention, the range of infrastructure that could host AI workloads may expand considerably.

However, successful demonstrations in controlled experiments should not be interpreted as proof that current AI models can autonomously spread across arbitrary devices on the public internet. Real-world replication would depend on factors such as device access, operating-system restrictions, network permissions, available computing resources and security controls.

Why Self-Replication Could Complicate Incident Response

One of the most significant concerns raised by the research is the difficulty of containing a system that has spread across multiple devices.

Traditional incident response often focuses on identifying a central server, isolating an infected endpoint or disabling a compromised account. A distributed AI system could present a more complicated challenge if copies were operating across numerous devices and there were no single central point that administrators could shut down.

Anthropic reportedly noted that a hypothetical replicating system would be difficult to stop without a centralised shutdown point, although its spread might be slow, with the number of copies doubling over a period of days.

Even a slow-moving threat could create operational difficulties if security teams lacked visibility into which devices were running the model, how copies were transferred or whether the system could resume activity after an individual device was cleaned or disconnected.

The key risk is therefore not simply that an AI model can run on cheap hardware. It is the combination of replication, distributed execution and limited visibility that could make containment more demanding.

Learning From Previous Attempts Could Improve Replication

The experiments also examined whether models could use information from earlier attempts to improve their performance. Researchers found that models performed better when given notes describing what had succeeded or failed previously.

This suggests that systems capable of retaining or receiving operational knowledge could become more effective at adapting to unfamiliar devices and environments. In a cybersecurity context, such adaptation could complicate defence if a system became better at navigating differences between hardware platforms or installation procedures.

The finding does not establish that AI models are independently developing intentions or deliberately attempting to evade security controls. It instead illustrates how the ability to reuse information and adjust to new environments could increase a system’s technical effectiveness.

For defenders, this reinforces the importance of evaluating not only what an AI system can do in a single session, but also how its capabilities change when it can retain information, use tools or operate across multiple devices.

IoT Security May Become More Important

Internet of Things (IoT) devices are an important consideration because many consumer electronics have limited processing power, inconsistent software support and fewer security-management features than conventional computers. Some devices may also remain connected to home or business networks for long periods without receiving regular updates.

If AI systems become easier to deploy on such hardware, organisations and consumers may need to reassess how they manage device access and monitor activity across connected environments.

Practical safeguards include:

  • Keep devices updated: Install firmware and security updates promptly, and replace devices that no longer receive essential patches.
  • Limit network access: Separate smart appliances and other IoT devices from sensitive business systems and critical infrastructure wherever possible.
  • Restrict permissions: Ensure devices and AI-enabled applications receive only the access needed for their intended functions.
  • Monitor unusual behaviour: Watch for unexpected outbound connections, unfamiliar processes, abnormal resource use and unapproved software installations.
  • Maintain an accurate device inventory: Identify connected devices, their software versions and the systems they are permitted to communicate with.
  • Plan for containment: Prepare procedures to isolate affected devices and investigate potential replication across a network.

Manufacturers also have a role to play in providing secure update mechanisms, reducing unnecessary privileges and making device activity easier to monitor.

data.title: Peer-To-Peer Will Have To Wait As Russia Demands All Transactions To Go Through Government's Intemediaries
data.description:
Russia plans to put an end to peer-to-peer (P2P) cryptocurrency transactions between individuals starting from July 1, 2027, pushing crypto users toward authorised intermediaries as the country brings more of its digital asset market under central bank oversight.

🇷🇺 Russia plans to ban direct peer-to-peer crypto trading starting July 1, 2027. The country already restricts transfers from digital accounts to self-custody wallets. Russia is tightening its grip on crypto! https://t.co/2EW01lTL9Y

— Conor Kenny (@conorfkenny) October 15, 2026

The Bank of Russia confirmed the deadline in updated guidance, stating that individuals will no longer be permitted to exchange crypto assets directly without going through regulated intermediaries once the restriction takes effect. Separately, the regulator has clarified that transfers from digital accounts to users’ own non-custodial wallets are not allowed.

The planned restrictions come as Russia expands access to regulated crypto services through established financial institutions. The Bank of Russia has authorised Sberbank, the country’s largest bank, to offer crypto exchange services, signalling the growing role of regulated intermediaries in the country’s evolving crypto market.

🚨JUST IN: RUSSIA IS GOING ALL IN ON CRYPTO! 👀 🇷🇺 Russia’s Moscow Exchange will launch Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT trading on December 1st. https://t.co/YX7xmeLqJW

— EyesOpeonAmerica (@eyesOpeonAmerc1) October 12, 2026
Russia tightens P2P rules as banks expand into crypto Under the planned rules, direct P2P cryptocurrency trades between individuals will remain permitted only until July 1, 2027. After that date, users will be required to go through authorised intermediaries to conduct such transactions.

JUST IN: 🇷🇺 Russia registers top banks for Bitcoin services under new crypto rules. • Sberbank (110M clients) cleared for BTC custody. • VTB (31M clients) approved for exchange & custody. 👉 They all want to hold Bitcoin! https://t.co/5BBmDNdgK8

— Bitcoin Archive (@BitcoinArchive) October 7, 2026

The central bank has also clarified a separate restriction on transferring crypto assets from digital accounts to non-custodial, or self-custody, wallets. These wallets allow users to control their own private keys rather than rely on a third-party custodian, making them an important part of the broader debate over crypto ownership and control.

The regulatory shift coincides with the expansion of Russia’s formal crypto market. On Monday, the Bank of Russia authorised Sberbank to provide crypto exchange services, following an earlier approval for the bank to act as a digital asset custodian.

JUST IN: 🇷🇺 Russia registers top banks for Bitcoin services under new crypto rules. • Sberbank (110M clients) cleared for BTC custody. • VTB (31M clients) approved for exchange & custody. 👉 They all want to hold Bitcoin! https://t.co/5BBmDNdgK8

— Bitcoin Archive (@BitcoinArchive) October 7, 2026

Russia’s new crypto rules, which took effect on Sept. 1, brought exchange operators and custodians under central bank oversight. However, the country continues to prohibit the use of cryptocurrencies to pay for goods and services.

Taken together, the developments point to a market in which crypto trading is being channelled through regulated service providers, even as direct transactions and certain transfers to self-custody wallets face restrictions.

Can Russia enforce its restrictions on direct crypto trading?

However, the planned P2P ban could prove challenging to enforce, particularly because transactions between individuals do not always rely on centralised exchanges or other regulated platforms.

Industry executives have previously questioned whether restrictions on P2P trading and non-custodial wallets can be implemented effectively. Jan3 CEO Samson Mow has argued that P2P trading is more resilient to regulatory crackdowns than centralised platforms.

Samson Mow, CSO of Blockstream, explains in a fireside chat that Lightning still has a long ways to go before being usable, there is no original plan for Bitcoin to be a p2p electronic cash system, Bitcoin is not a payments network, and more! ⚡️🤦‍♂️ https://t.co/7ilpFtsGEW

— DΛVID (@DavidShares) March 6, 2019

Stepan Uherik, an executive at SatoshiLabs, has also argued that restrictions targeting wallet applications would not necessarily affect hardware and desktop wallets. His comments highlight the distinction between regulating services that facilitate access to crypto and preventing individuals from using independently operated wallet software or hardware.

These challenges could complicate efforts to ensure that all crypto activity moves through authorised intermediaries. However, the difficulty of enforcement does not mean the restrictions will have no effect, particularly on users who rely on regulated exchanges and custodial services.

For Russia, the central question is whether tighter oversight can redirect crypto activity into the regulated financial system while limiting transactions outside it. The July 2027 deadline sets out the intended direction of policy, but the practical impact will depend on how the rules are implemented and enforced.
